questions.question: Define refraction and explain why it happens. State the direction a ray bends when it passes from air into glass, from glass into air, and along the normal.
questions.expected_answer: Refraction is the change in direction of light as it passes at an angle from one transparent medium into another. It happens because light changes speed: about 300 000 km/s in air, about 225 000 km/s in water and about 200 000 km/s in glass. Air into glass: light slows down and bends towards the normal (angle of refraction smaller than angle of incidence). Glass into air: light speeds up and bends away from the normal. Along the normal (angle of incidence 0°): speed changes but direction does not; the ray passes straight through.

questions.question: Explain why a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is and why this can be dangerous. Explain how a mirage forms on a hot road.
questions.expected_answer: Light from the bottom of the pool bends away from the normal as it leaves the water into the air. The eye and brain trace the light back in straight lines, so the bottom appears higher than it really is (about three quarters of the real depth). People may misjudge the depth of pools, rivers and dams and get into difficulty. Mirage: air just above hot tar is hotter and less dense than air higher up; light from the sky travelling downwards is gradually refracted upwards through the layers of hotter air and reaches the eye from below; the brain sees an image of the sky on the road, which looks like a pool of water.

questions.question: Describe the shapes and effects on parallel light of convex and concave lenses. Explain how a convex lens can be used as a magnifying glass and how spectacles correct short sight.
questions.expected_answer: Convex (converging) lens: thicker in the middle; parallel rays are refracted towards the axis and converge at the principal focus (focal point); can form real, inverted images. Concave (diverging) lens: thinner in the middle; parallel rays spread out as if from a focal point on the near side; forms smaller, upright, virtual images. Magnifying glass: an object placed closer to a convex lens than its focal length gives an upright, enlarged, virtual image seen through the lens. Short sight: light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina; a concave lens diverges the light slightly before it enters the eye so it focuses on the retina.
